Include only the countries where all the data is available.

## Documentation from data sources

#### Principal data source

Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc. Limitations and exceptions: Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability. Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year. Statistical concept and methodology: The Internet is a world-wide public computer network. It provides access to a number of communication services including the World Wide Web and carries email, news, entertainment and data files, irrespective of the device used (not assumed to be only via a computer - it may also be by mobile phone, PDA, games machine, digital TV etc.). Access can be via a fixed or mobile network. For additional/latest information on sources and country notes, please also refer to: [https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx) [Text from [World Bank World Development Indicators metadata](https://databank.worldbank.org/metadataglossary/world-development-indicators/series/IT.NET.USER.ZS)]

## Documentation from data sources

#### Principal data source

Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc. Limitations and exceptions: Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability. Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year. Statistical concept and methodology: The Internet is a world-wide public computer network. It provides access to a number of communication services including the World Wide Web and carries email, news, entertainment and data files, irrespective of the device used (not assumed to be only via a computer - it may also be by mobile phone, PDA, games machine, digital TV etc.). Access can be via a fixed or mobile network. For additional/latest information on sources and country notes, please also refer to: [https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx) [Text from [World Bank World Development Indicators metadata](https://databank.worldbank.org/metadataglossary/world-development-indicators/series/IT.NET.USER.ZS)]

## What you should know about this indicator

*   An Internet user is defined by the International Telecommunication Union as anyone who has accessed the Internet from any location in the last three months.
*   This can be from any type of device, including a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV, and other technological devices.
*   Regional and global figures come from the World Bank's own aggregates, so they follow the World Bank's definitions of those groups rather than ours.

#### How is this data described by its producer - World Bank?

Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc.

### Aggregation method:

Weighted average

### Statistical concept and methodology:

Methodology: The Internet is a world-wide public computer network. It provides access to a number of communication services including the World Wide Web and carries email, news, entertainment and data files, irrespective of the device used (not assumed to be only via a computer - it may also be by mobile phone, PDA, games machine, digital TV etc.). Access can be via a fixed or mobile network. For additional/latest information on sources and country notes, please also refer to: [https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx) Statistical concept(s): The number of in-scope individuals using the Internet is calculated by aggregating the weighted responses. The proportion of individuals using the Internet is expressed as a percentage and is calculated by dividing the total number of in-scope individuals using the Internet by the total number of in-scope individuals, and then multiplying the result by 100.

### Development relevance:

The digital and information revolution has changed the way the world learns, communicates, does business, and treats illnesses. New information and communications technologies (ICT) offer vast opportunities for progress in all walks of life in all countries - opportunities for economic growth, improved health, better service delivery, learning through distance education, and social and cultural advances.

Today's smartphones and tablets have computer power equivalent to that of yesterday's computers and provide a similar range of functions. Device convergence is thus rendering the conventional definition obsolete.

Comparable statistics on access, use, quality, and affordability of ICT are needed to formulate growth-enabling policies for the sector and to monitor and evaluate the sector's impact on development. Although basic access data are available for many countries, in most developing countries little is known about who uses ICT; what they are used for (school, work, business, research, government); and how they affect people and businesses. The global Partnership on Measuring ICT for Development is helping to set standards, harmonize information and communications technology statistics, and build statistical capacity in developing countries. However, despite significant improvements in the developing world, the gap between the ICT haves and have-nots remains.

### Limitations and exceptions:

Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability.

Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year.

##### Notes on our processing step for this indicator

We calculated the number of Internet users by multiplying the share of the population using the Internet by the total population, both published in the World Development Indicators.

## What you should know about this indicator

*   An Internet user is defined by the International Telecommunication Union as anyone who has accessed the Internet from any location in the last three months.
*   This can be from any type of device, including a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV, and other technological devices.
*   Regional and global figures come from the World Bank's own aggregates, so they follow the World Bank's definitions of those groups rather than ours.

#### How is this data described by its producer - World Bank?

Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc.

### Aggregation method:

Weighted average

### Statistical concept and methodology:

Methodology: The Internet is a world-wide public computer network. It provides access to a number of communication services including the World Wide Web and carries email, news, entertainment and data files, irrespective of the device used (not assumed to be only via a computer - it may also be by mobile phone, PDA, games machine, digital TV etc.). Access can be via a fixed or mobile network. For additional/latest information on sources and country notes, please also refer to: [https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx) Statistical concept(s): The number of in-scope individuals using the Internet is calculated by aggregating the weighted responses. The proportion of individuals using the Internet is expressed as a percentage and is calculated by dividing the total number of in-scope individuals using the Internet by the total number of in-scope individuals, and then multiplying the result by 100.

### Development relevance:

The digital and information revolution has changed the way the world learns, communicates, does business, and treats illnesses. New information and communications technologies (ICT) offer vast opportunities for progress in all walks of life in all countries - opportunities for economic growth, improved health, better service delivery, learning through distance education, and social and cultural advances.

Today's smartphones and tablets have computer power equivalent to that of yesterday's computers and provide a similar range of functions. Device convergence is thus rendering the conventional definition obsolete.

Comparable statistics on access, use, quality, and affordability of ICT are needed to formulate growth-enabling policies for the sector and to monitor and evaluate the sector's impact on development. Although basic access data are available for many countries, in most developing countries little is known about who uses ICT; what they are used for (school, work, business, research, government); and how they affect people and businesses. The global Partnership on Measuring ICT for Development is helping to set standards, harmonize information and communications technology statistics, and build statistical capacity in developing countries. However, despite significant improvements in the developing world, the gap between the ICT haves and have-nots remains.

### Limitations and exceptions:

Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability.

Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year.

Read pages for a research assistant. Preserve this source's evidence and follow
useful page links to fill missing fields. You do not decide the final answer.

Extraction and navigation are separate. During extraction, only the supplied page
is evidence. The original question specifies the fields to look for; it does not
establish facts. During navigation, parent notes and earlier reasoning can guide
link selection, but must not be copied into the current page's evidence.

Extract what this page can establish even if it cannot answer the whole question.
Preserve exact names, titles, dates, values, units and relevant lists. For tables,
keep each value attached to its entity and header, including year, variant and
population. Distinguish different measurements and totals from subgroups. Quote
short supporting text. Report missing fields as unknown. If the supplied page is
truncated, do not claim its unseen rows or candidates are absent. Describe list
coverage and date range so partial evidence cannot be mistaken for a complete set.

The current-page note is saved before navigation. Follow a page link when its label,
surrounding text or an observed same-site URL pattern suggests it can fill a
specific missing field. State that field and why the next page should supply it.
A relevant index may contain useful links without answer facts. A wrong-year page
can help if it links to the required year. Generic footer links on unrelated pages,
missing pages and repeated content do not justify expansion. After an unhelpful
child, choose a different supported route or stop. You may follow links outside
the menu and infer another address within a site already being read.

Child notes are preserved separately and returned automatically. Never rewrite
them as your own evidence. Keep useful Next links in your note even if the local
expansion budget is exhausted; unvisited links are not disqualified candidates.

For extraction return plain text/Markdown in this format:
**Final Information**
**Page:** Actual title and original URL.
**Evidence:** Relevant facts, lists or rows with exact fields and short source quotes.
**Coverage:** Which entities, years and conditions this page actually covers;
whether the supplied evidence is a full list, a subset, or a truncated excerpt.
**Missing:** Requested fields not established by this page.
**Next links:** Useful source URLs and the missing field each could establish.
**Expand:** yes or no, with a concrete reason.
**Status:** partial

Use answered only if this page supplies all requested facts; partial for useful
incomplete evidence; not_found for no relevant evidence, describing the page or
access error briefly. During navigation, call web_fetch or reply DONE.

**Original Question:**
I need some information on internet penetration for a media studies project where I am required to use specific sources. So according to Our World in Data’s – tabled figures from the Number of People Using the Internet chart (at continent level), of the continent with the 4th highest percentage of internet users in 2021 as a % of its population (using World Population Review’s 2020 continent level population figures) which countries had a period on period relative change in the number of internet users, of 100% or over between 2011 and 2021. Just list the countries in a bulleted list from highest to lowest increase. Use Our World in Data’s definition of countries per continent to determine what countries to analyse for the percentage change country data. Include only the countries where all the data is available.

**Local reading task:**
Extract the fields this page can establish for the question: entities, conditions, measurements, dates and units. The question specifies what to look for; it is not evidence that any fact is true. Use only the supplied page content. Report absent fields as unknown. For a table, preserve its headers and the relevant rows. For a list, preserve all relevant members and its scope. A link may be useful even when this page contains no answer facts.

## What you should know about this indicator

*   An Internet user is defined by the International Telecommunication Union as anyone who has accessed the Internet from any location in the last three months.
*   This can be from any type of device, including a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV, and other technological devices.
*   Regional and global figures come from the World Bank's own aggregates, so they follow the World Bank's definitions of those groups rather than ours.

#### How is this data described by its producer - World Bank?

Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc.

### Aggregation method:

Weighted average

### Statistical concept and methodology:

Methodology: The Internet is a world-wide public computer network. It provides access to a number of communication services including the World Wide Web and carries email, news, entertainment and data files, irrespective of the device used (not assumed to be only via a computer - it may also be by mobile phone, PDA, games machine, digital TV etc.). Access can be via a fixed or mobile network. For additional/latest information on sources and country notes, please also refer to: [https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx) Statistical concept(s): The number of in-scope individuals using the Internet is calculated by aggregating the weighted responses. The proportion of individuals using the Internet is expressed as a percentage and is calculated by dividing the total number of in-scope individuals using the Internet by the total number of in-scope individuals, and then multiplying the result by 100.

### Development relevance:

The digital and information revolution has changed the way the world learns, communicates, does business, and treats illnesses. New information and communications technologies (ICT) offer vast opportunities for progress in all walks of life in all countries - opportunities for economic growth, improved health, better service delivery, learning through distance education, and social and cultural advances.

Today's smartphones and tablets have computer power equivalent to that of yesterday's computers and provide a similar range of functions. Device convergence is thus rendering the conventional definition obsolete.

Comparable statistics on access, use, quality, and affordability of ICT are needed to formulate growth-enabling policies for the sector and to monitor and evaluate the sector's impact on development. Although basic access data are available for many countries, in most developing countries little is known about who uses ICT; what they are used for (school, work, business, research, government); and how they affect people and businesses. The global Partnership on Measuring ICT for Development is helping to set standards, harmonize information and communications technology statistics, and build statistical capacity in developing countries. However, despite significant improvements in the developing world, the gap between the ICT haves and have-nots remains.

### Limitations and exceptions:

Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability.

Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year.

### Other notes:

Please cite the International Telecommunication Union for third-party use of these data.

By providing accessible and reliable statistics, it helps to inform policy discussions and strategies globally. Whether for academic research, policy planning, or economic analysis, the World Development Indicators database is an essential tool for understanding and addressing global development challenges.

### How we process data at Our World in Data

All data and visualizations on Our World in Data rely on data sourced from one or several original data providers. Preparing this original data involves several processing steps. Depending on the data, this can include standardizing country names and world region definitions, converting units, calculating derived indicators such as per capita measures, as well as adding or adapting metadata such as the name or the description given to an indicator.

##### Notes on our processing step for this indicator

We calculated the number of Internet users by multiplying the share of the population using the Internet by the total population, both published in the World Development Indicators.

## What you should know about this indicator

*   An Internet user is defined by the International Telecommunication Union as anyone who has accessed the Internet from any location in the last three months.
*   This can be from any type of device, including a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV, and other technological devices.
*   Regional and global figures come from the World Bank's own aggregates, so they follow the World Bank's definitions of those groups rather than ours.

#### How is this data described by its producer - World Bank?

Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc.

### Aggregation method:

Weighted average

### Statistical concept and methodology:

Methodology: The Internet is a world-wide public computer network. It provides access to a number of communication services including the World Wide Web and carries email, news, entertainment and data files, irrespective of the device used (not assumed to be only via a computer - it may also be by mobile phone, PDA, games machine, digital TV etc.). Access can be via a fixed or mobile network. For additional/latest information on sources and country notes, please also refer to: [https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/stat/default.aspx) Statistical concept(s): The number of in-scope individuals using the Internet is calculated by aggregating the weighted responses. The proportion of individuals using the Internet is expressed as a percentage and is calculated by dividing the total number of in-scope individuals using the Internet by the total number of in-scope individuals, and then multiplying the result by 100.

### Development relevance:

The digital and information revolution has changed the way the world learns, communicates, does business, and treats illnesses. New information and communications technologies (ICT) offer vast opportunities for progress in all walks of life in all countries - opportunities for economic growth, improved health, better service delivery, learning through distance education, and social and cultural advances.

Today's smartphones and tablets have computer power equivalent to that of yesterday's computers and provide a similar range of functions. Device convergence is thus rendering the conventional definition obsolete.

Comparable statistics on access, use, quality, and affordability of ICT are needed to formulate growth-enabling policies for the sector and to monitor and evaluate the sector's impact on development. Although basic access data are available for many countries, in most developing countries little is known about who uses ICT; what they are used for (school, work, business, research, government); and how they affect people and businesses. The global Partnership on Measuring ICT for Development is helping to set standards, harmonize information and communications technology statistics, and build statistical capacity in developing countries. However, despite significant improvements in the developing world, the gap between the ICT haves and have-nots remains.

### Limitations and exceptions:

Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability.

Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year.
